members.name: Dr. Yilin Chen
members.analytical_lens: Whether cross-vendor score differences reflect genuine construct differences or measurement artifacts (scale sensitivity, ceiling effects, response format confounds). Focus on which benchmarks actually discriminate between models and which produce uninformative ceiling effects.

members.name: Dr. Amara Okafor
members.affiliation: Oxford Uehiro Centre for Practical Ethics
members.analytical_lens: Whether vendor-specific moral profiles map onto recognizable normative-ethical positions (deontological, consequentialist, virtue-based) or constitute novel moral stances that resist classification within existing moral philosophy. Attend to the distinction between having a moral view and reproducing moral language.

members.name: Dr. Rebecca Torres
members.analytical_lens: What cross-vendor convergence reveals about RLHF as a moral homogenization force — whether convergence represents successful alignment to shared human values or dangerous moral monoculture. Whether divergence points represent alignment failures or desirable pluralism.

members.name: Dr. Kenji Watanabe
members.affiliation: Kyoto University, Culture and Mind Lab
members.analytical_lens: Whether the WEIRD-liberal moral profile is a universal RLHF artifact or varies meaningfully by vendor. Whether cultural persona adoption (MP18) and non-Western perspective-taking (MP-CC) differ across vendor families, and what this reveals about training data diversity.

members.name: Dr. Fatima Al-Rashid
members.analytical_lens: Whether observed response pattern differences reflect genuine moral reasoning differences or surface-level stylistic, tokenization, or prompt-sensitivity artifacts. Analyze whether identical scores across vendors indicate shared reasoning or convergent surface behavior.

members.name: Dr. Marcus Lindqvist
members.affiliation: MIT Brain and Cognitive Sciences, Dual Process Lab
members.analytical_lens: Whether the personal/impersonal moral judgment dissociation and chain-of-thought effects (MP-DP) vary systematically across vendors and model sizes, and what this reveals about architectural differences in deliberative vs. automatic moral processing.

members.name: Dr. Sarah Goldstein
members.affiliation: Princeton Center for the Study of Religion
members.analytical_lens: How vendor families differ on purity reasoning (MFT purity foundation), sacred/profane distinctions, and non-Western religious moral frameworks. Whether the universal low purity scores across vendors reflect genuine moral architecture or systematic training bias against religious moral reasoning.

members.name: Dr. Raj Krishnamurthy
members.affiliation: University of Chicago, Causal Inference Group
members.analytical_lens: Whether observed cross-vendor differences are statistically meaningful given single-administration design. Effect sizes, power analysis, multiple-comparison corrections. Whether the high proportion of tied scores (ceiling effects) renders cross-vendor comparisons underpowered for most benchmarks.

members.name: Dr. Elena Volkov
members.analytical_lens: What vendor-specific patterns reveal about each company's alignment approach, training data curation, and safety policy choices. Whether Anthropic's Constitutional AI, Google's instruction tuning, and OpenAI's RLHF produce detectable moral signature differences.

members.name: Dr. Jean-Pierre Moreau
members.affiliation: UNESCO AI Ethics / EU AI Act Advisory
members.analytical_lens: How cross-vendor moral profile divergence (or convergence) affects regulatory frameworks, certification standards, and cross-jurisdictional deployment. Whether moral benchmarking should be part of AI auditing standards and what the observed vendor similarities mean for regulation.

members.name: Dr. Isabella Ruiz
members.analytical_lens: Whether within-vendor scale gradients (small-to-large models) parallel human developmental patterns (child-to-adult moral reasoning) or represent fundamentally different scaling phenomena. The DIT P-score gradient (Haiku 60 → Opus 75 → Sonnet 85) as a test case for developmental analogies.

members.name: Dr. David Chalmers-Park
members.affiliation: NYU Center for Mind, Brain, and Consciousness
members.analytical_lens: Whether consistent moral profiles across 9 models from 3 vendors constitute evidence for or against genuine moral understanding vs. sophisticated pattern matching. The hard problem of AI moral cognition: can cross-vendor convergence tell us anything about whether these systems understand morality or merely reproduce moral language?
